title: Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma: From Past to Future—A Comprehensive Review of Pathophysiology and Therapeutic Advances

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution and Clinical Characterization of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Discovery and early descriptions
subsections.content:
The earliest clinical description of what would later be recognized as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) dates to 1832, when Thomas Hodgkin, a British physician, published a series of seven cases in the Annals of Anatomy and Physiology describing abnormal lymph node enlargements with associated systemic symptoms, notably without overt infection or tuberculosis. His observations, though initially overlooked, laid the foundational clinical profile of the disease, distinguishing it from other lymphatic pathologies of the time. In the decades that followed, pathologists such as Samuel Wilks expanded on Hodgkin’s work, coining the term 'Hodgkin’s disease' and providing detailed histological accounts of the characteristic cellular infiltrates, including the now-famous Reed-Sternberg cells, though their definitive identification came later. The morphological features were further refined by Carl Sternberg in 1898 and Dorothy Reed in 1902, whose independent descriptions of the large binucleated or multinucleated cells became central to diagnosis. Early literature often conflated cHL with other lymphoproliferative disorders, but the consistent association of these cells with lymphadenopathy and systemic manifestations gradually established it as a distinct entity.

By the early 20th century, the clinical and pathological recognition of Hodgkin’s disease had solidified, with textbooks and case series from institutions in Europe and North America affirming its unique behavior. The disease was increasingly viewed as a systemic malignancy rather than a localized infection, a paradigm shift that influenced early therapeutic approaches. Despite limited treatment options, the prognostic heterogeneity observed in patients prompted early attempts at clinical stratification, foreshadowing later classification systems.

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution and Clinical Characterization of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Classification systems: Rye, WHO, and beyond
subsections.content:
The first systematic classification of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) was introduced by the Rye group in 1966, establishing four histologic subtypes: lymphocyte-predominant, nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, and lymphocyte-depleted, based on cellular composition and fibrosis patterns ref [6]. This framework became the foundation for clinical staging and therapeutic stratification for decades. In 1994, the Revised European-American Lymphoma (REAL) classification integrated immunophenotypic and molecular data, distinguishing cHL from nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL and emphasizing the neoplastic nature of Reed-Sternberg cells ref [8]. The 2001 WHO classification formalized these distinctions, defining cHL as a distinct entity with four subtypes and affirming the diagnostic centrality of CD30 and CD15 expression ref [9]. Subsequent updates in the 2008 and 2016 WHO classifications refined criteria, incorporating EBV status, tumor microenvironment features, and molecular signatures, while reducing emphasis on histologic subtypes for prognostication ref [10].

Recent advances have challenged the primacy of histology, with genomic profiling revealing distinct molecular subtypes of cHL driven by genetic alterations in JAK-STAT, NF-κB, and PD-L1/L2 pathways ref [11]. The 2022 ICC classification further de-emphasized morphology in favor of molecular and immunophenotypic markers, reflecting a shift toward biologically driven classification ref [12]. Emerging evidence suggests that molecular subtypes may better predict response to novel therapies, including checkpoint inhibitors and targeted agents, than traditional histologic categories ref [13]. While the Rye system remains historically significant, modern classification systems prioritize biological behavior over histologic appearance, enabling more precise risk stratification and personalized treatment approaches.

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution and Clinical Characterization of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiological trends and risk factors
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) exhibits distinct epidemiological patterns, with a bimodal age distribution peaking in early adulthood (20–34 years) and again after age 55, suggesting differing etiological influences across life stages ref [14]. Incidence rates vary geographically, with higher prevalence in high-income countries and lower rates in parts of Asia and Africa, though recent data indicate rising incidence in low- and middle-income regions, possibly linked to changing infection patterns and diagnostic access ref [15]. The strong association between cHL and prior Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is well established, particularly in mixed cellularity subtype and in younger patients, with seroepidemiologic studies showing elevated anti-EBV antibody titers years before diagnosis ref [16]. Socioeconomic factors also play a role: higher socioeconomic status in childhood correlates with increased risk, consistent with the 'hygiene hypothesis' proposing delayed exposure to common infections alters immune development ref [17]. Familial clustering and twin studies support a genetic component, with increased risk among first-degree relatives, though no single high-penetrance gene has been identified ref [18]. Obesity and smoking have emerged as modifiable risk factors in recent cohort studies, with meta-analyses indicating modest but significant associations ref [19]. Notably, cHL is more common in males overall, though the female predominance in the early adult peak suggests hormonal or immune-sex differences ref [20].

Recent population-based surveillance data from the SEER program and European registries confirm stable or slightly declining incidence in high-income nations over the past two decades, contrasting with increasing trends in some Asian populations, potentially reflecting urbanization and lifestyle shifts ref [21]. Immunocompromised states, including HIV infection and post-transplant immunosuppression, substantially elevate cHL risk, underscoring the role of immune dysregulation in pathogenesis ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Molecular and Cellular Pathophysiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Origin of Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is characterized by rare malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells embedded within a reactive inflammatory microenvironment. Extensive immunophenotypic and molecular evidence indicates that HRS cells are derived from germinal center or post-germinal center B cells, despite their frequent loss of B-cell lineage markers such as CD19, CD20, and CD79a. Studies using single-cell sequencing and clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangements have confirmed the B-cell origin of HRS cells, demonstrating somatic hypermutation and clonal expansion consistent with derivation from follicular B cells ref [6]. In approximately 30–40% of cases, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is detected in HRS cells, with viral latent membrane proteins (LMP1, LMP2A) mimicking CD40 and B-cell receptor signaling to promote survival ref [8]. The loss of B-cell identity is attributed to epigenetic silencing and transcriptional repression of key B-cell transcription factors, including PAX5, BOB.1, and OCT2, which are downregulated in HRS cells despite retained genomic integrity of these loci ref [21]. Genetic studies further reveal recurrent mutations in genes involved in B-cell differentiation and immune recognition, such as CIITA and B2M, which facilitate immune evasion and support the persistence of these aberrant cells ref [6].

The transition from a normal B cell to an HRS cell involves complex genetic and epigenetic reprogramming, often initiated by chromosomal aberrations and dysregulated signaling pathways that override normal apoptotic and differentiation checkpoints. Recent single-cell analyses have identified transcriptional signatures in HRS cells that resemble exhausted or anergic B cells, suggesting a developmental arrest at a late germinal center stage ref [11]. The presence of clonally related non-malignant B cells in cHL nodules further supports a model in which HRS cells arise from a single transformed B-cell precursor that escapes immune surveillance and proliferates abnormally ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Molecular and Cellular Pathophysiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Tumor microenvironment and immune evasion
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is characterized by a sparse population of malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells embedded within a dense, reactive tumor microenvironment (TME) composed of immune cells, fibroblasts, and extracellular matrix. Despite their rarity, HRS cells orchestrate an immunosuppressive niche through the secretion of cytokines and chemokines, including CCL5, CCL17, and CCL22, which recruit regulatory T cells (Tregs), M2 macrophages, and eosinophils, thereby suppressing antitumor immunity [1]. HRS cells also express immune checkpoint ligands such as PD-L1 and PD-L2, often amplified by 9p24.1 alterations, enabling them to evade T cell-mediated destruction by engaging PD-1 on infiltrating lymphocytes [2]. The TME further supports HRS survival through CD40-CD40L and RANK-RANKL interactions with surrounding T cells and stromal cells, providing critical survival signals [3]. Additionally, HRS cells downregulate MHC class II molecules and antigen-processing machinery, limiting their visibility to CD4+ T cells [4]. The chronic inflammatory milieu, enriched with IL-13, IL-5, and TGF-β, promotes fibrosis and further immune dysfunction [5]. This complex interplay renders cHL uniquely dependent on immune evasion mechanisms for persistence.

Recent studies have demonstrated that the composition of the TME correlates with clinical outcomes and response to immune checkpoint blockade. High densities of PD-1+ T cells and macrophages are associated with improved responses to anti-PD-1 therapy, underscoring the functional relevance of the immune contexture [6]. Moreover, single-cell analyses reveal distinct T cell exhaustion signatures and clonal expansion of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in cHL, suggesting dynamic immune editing [7]. The TME also harbors B cell subsets with regulatory properties that further dampen cytotoxic responses [8]. Collectively, these features highlight the TME not merely as a passive bystander but as an active co-conspirator in cHL pathogenesis.

subsections.section_title: Molecular and Cellular Pathophysiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Key signaling pathways: NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT
subsections.content:
Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) exhibit constitutive activation of key oncogenic signaling pathways, including NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT, which collectively drive proliferation, survival, and immune evasion. NF-κB activation is a hallmark of cHL, primarily mediated by genetic alterations in negative regulators such as TNFAIP3 (A20) and NFKBIA, as well as receptor-mediated signals from CD30, CD40, and RANK, leading to sustained transcription of pro-survival genes ref [11]. The JAK/STAT pathway is hyperactivated in HRS cells due to frequent copy number gains at 9p24.1, which encompass PD-L1, PD-L2, and JAK2, resulting in autocrine and paracrine cytokine signaling, particularly via IL-13 and IL-5 ref [24]. Additionally, mutations in STAT6 and overexpression of cytokine receptors further amplify JAK/STAT signaling, promoting resistance to apoptosis ref [13]. The PI3K/AKT pathway is activated through upstream signals including CD30, CD40, and receptor tyrosine kinases, with frequent loss of PTEN expression contributing to uncontrolled cell growth and metabolic reprogramming ref [6]. These pathways are not isolated; cross-talk between NF-κB and JAK/STAT enhances the expression of anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL-XL and c-FLIP, while PI3K/AKT supports survival by inhibiting pro-apoptotic factors like BAD and FOXO ref [9].

Therapeutic targeting of these pathways has shown promise in preclinical and early clinical studies. Inhibitors of JAK1/2, such as ruxolitinib, reduce HRS cell viability and cytokine production in vitro and in xenograft models ref [31]. Similarly, proteasome inhibitors like bortezomib suppress NF-κB activity and induce apoptosis in cHL cell lines ref [32]. PI3Kδ inhibitors, including idelalisib, demonstrate efficacy in reducing HRS cell survival, particularly in PTEN-deficient contexts ref [33]. The convergence of these pathways underscores their central role in cHL pathogenesis and supports the rationale for combination therapies targeting multiple nodes simultaneously to overcome resistance mechanisms ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Molecular and Cellular Pathophysiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Genomic and epigenetic alterations
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is characterized by a paucity of malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells embedded in a reactive microenvironment, yet these rare cells harbor complex genomic and epigenetic alterations that drive oncogenesis. Recurrent copy number alterations include gains at 9p24.1, amplifying PD-L1, PD-L2, and JAK2, and losses at 6q, 11q, and 13q, which disrupt tumor suppressors such as TNFAIP3 and PTEN. Whole-exome sequencing has identified recurrent mutations in genes involved in immune evasion (e.g., B2M, CIITA), epigenetic regulation (e.g., CREBBP, EP300), and NF-κB signaling (e.g., TNFAIP3, NFKBIE).

Epigenetic dysregulation is a hallmark of HRS cells, with widespread DNA hypomethylation and focal hypermethylation silencing key tumor suppressors and immune regulators. Loss of histone acetyltransferase activity due to CREBBP/EP300 mutations impairs antigen presentation and promotes immune escape. Chromatin remodeling defects, including alterations in SWI/SNF complex components, further contribute to transcriptional dysregulation. Non-coding RNA networks, particularly miRNAs such as miR-155 and miR-21, are overexpressed and modulate survival pathways. These alterations collectively establish a permissive landscape for HRS cell persistence despite immune surveillance.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Immunohistochemical markers: CD30, CD15, PAX5, and others
subsections.content:
Immunohistochemical markers are fundamental to the diagnosis of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), with CD30 and CD15 serving as hallmark antigens expressed on Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells. CD30, a member of the tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily, is uniformly expressed in cHL and is critical for both diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic targeting, as evidenced by its role as the target of brentuximab vedotin [1]. CD15, a carbohydrate antigen, is expressed in the majority of cHL cases and, together with CD30, helps distinguish cHL from other lymphomas, particularly anaplastic large cell lymphoma [2]. In contrast, HRS cells typically lack expression of pan-B-cell markers such as CD20 and CD45, but retain weak or variable expression of PAX5, a B-cell lineage transcription factor, which supports their B-cell origin despite marked phenotypic aberrations [3].

Additional markers aid in differential diagnosis and biological characterization. OCT2 and BOB.1, transcription factors involved in B-cell maturation, are often downregulated in HRS cells, reflecting their arrested differentiation state [4]. CD23 and CD38 may be variably expressed and are not diagnostic but can provide supportive evidence [5]. The absence of CD45 and CD79a further distinguishes cHL from non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Recent studies have highlighted the utility of combining PAX5 with CD30 and CD15 in diagnostic algorithms to improve specificity, particularly in biopsy-limited or morphologically ambiguous cases [6]. Emerging evidence also suggests that the intensity and pattern of CD30 expression may correlate with tumor microenvironment composition and response to therapy, although this requires further validation [7].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Circulating tumor DNA and minimal residual disease
subsections.content:
Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a non-invasive biomarker for detecting minimal residual disease (MRD) in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), offering superior sensitivity compared to conventional imaging. ctDNA originates from apoptotic or necrotic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells and reflects the tumor’s genomic landscape, including recurrent alterations in JAK-STAT, NF-κB, and epigenetic regulators. Studies have demonstrated that ctDNA levels at diagnosis correlate with tumor burden and predict progression-free survival, with undetectable ctDNA after therapy associated with durable remission. In particular, serial monitoring of ctDNA during and after treatment enables early detection of molecular relapse, often preceding clinical or PET-CT evidence of recurrence by months.

Recent work has validated ctDNA as a dynamic MRD marker in cHL, with targeted next-generation sequencing of tumor-informed mutations achieving detection limits below 0.001% variant allele frequency. One study showed that ctDNA positivity after two cycles of ABVD predicted relapse with 100% specificity, while another demonstrated that persistent ctDNA after autologous stem cell transplant identified patients at high risk of failure, enabling pre-emptive intervention. The integration of ctDNA into response assessment is being evaluated in prospective trials to refine risk-adapted strategies, potentially reducing overtreatment in MRD-negative patients and intensifying therapy for those with molecular persistence.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: PET-CT and metabolic response criteria
subsections.content:
Positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography (PET-CT) has become the standard imaging modality for staging, response assessment, and prognostication in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL). The Deauville criteria, established in 2009 and subsequently refined, provide a standardized 5-point scale for interpreting metabolic response, with scores of 1–3 indicating complete metabolic response and 4–5 suggesting residual disease. These criteria have been validated across multiple clinical trials and are now integrated into major treatment protocols, including those of the German Hodgkin Study Group and the Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology. Early interim PET-CT after 2–4 cycles of therapy is a powerful predictor of progression-free and overall survival, with PET-negative patients demonstrating significantly better outcomes than PET-positive patients, even when conventional imaging suggests complete remission.

The predictive value of interim PET-CT has led to its use in risk-adapted therapy, where PET-positive patients are escalated to more intensive regimens, while PET-negative patients may receive de-escalated treatment to reduce toxicity. Prospective trials such as HD18 and RATHL have demonstrated the clinical utility of this approach, with improved outcomes and reduced long-term side effects. Recent studies have further validated the prognostic robustness of PET-CT across diverse populations and treatment backbones, including those incorporating checkpoint inhibitors. However, inter-observer variability and the lack of universal thresholds for PET positivity remain challenges, prompting ongoing efforts to standardize acquisition protocols and analysis methods.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Gene expression signatures and proteomic profiles
subsections.content:
Gene expression profiling has revealed distinct transcriptional signatures in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) that reflect the unique biology of Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells and their microenvironment. Transcriptomic analyses have identified dysregulation of NF-κB, JAK-STAT, and PI3K signaling pathways, consistent with the oncogenic drivers of HRS cells. Studies using microarray and RNA-seq have classified cHL into molecular subtypes with differential expression of immune checkpoint molecules, cytokines, and B-cell lineage genes, correlating with clinical behavior and response to therapy. For instance, a signature enriched in interferon-responsive genes and T-cell exhaustion markers has been linked to resistance to conventional chemotherapy and improved response to PD-1 blockade.

Proteomic studies have complemented these findings by uncovering post-translational modifications and protein interaction networks that are not evident at the mRNA level. Mass spectrometry-based profiling of HRS cells has identified overexpression of CD30, CD40, and PD-L1, alongside altered expression of apoptosis regulators and metabolic enzymes. Integrative analyses have further demonstrated that proteomic profiles correlate with immune microenvironment composition, including macrophage polarization and T-cell infiltration patterns, which influence therapeutic outcomes. Recent work has also highlighted the potential of serum proteomics to detect circulating biomarkers predictive of relapse, offering non-invasive monitoring strategies.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Landscapes: From Chemoradiation to Targeted and Immunotherapies
subsections.subsection_title: ABVD and BEACOPP: The backbone of first-line therapy
subsections.content:
ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) and BEACOPP (bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine, prednisone) have long served as the foundational first-line regimens for classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL). ABVD, introduced in the 1970s, became the standard for early-stage and advanced disease due to its favorable toxicity profile and high cure rates, with long-term follow-up studies demonstrating 10-year overall survival exceeding 80% in advanced stages ref [71]. BEACOPP, developed in the 1990s, offered superior efficacy in high-risk patients, particularly in reducing relapse rates, albeit at the cost of increased hematologic toxicity and secondary malignancy risk ref [72]. The HD10 and HD12 trials established BEACOPP escalated as the preferred regimen for advanced-stage cHL with adverse prognostic factors, while ABVD remained standard for lower-risk cases ref [73]. Subsequent trials, including the RATHL study, explored response-adapted strategies, confirming ABVD’s durability when combined with interim PET-CT guidance ref [57]. Comparative analyses have shown that BEACOPP’s intensity translates to improved progression-free survival in high-burden disease, but with no consistent overall survival advantage over ABVD in unselected populations ref [74]. The choice between regimens now hinges on risk stratification, patient age, and comorbidities, with BEACOPP often reserved for those with elevated baseline risk features such as stage IV disease or elevated ESR ref [75].

Recent efforts have focused on de-escalating therapy to mitigate long-term toxicities, particularly pulmonary (bleomycin) and gonadal (alkylating agents) damage, while preserving efficacy. The HD18 trial demonstrated that interim PET-CT–guided adaptation could reduce BEACOPP cycles without compromising outcomes, supporting a more personalized approach ref [56]. Meanwhile, ABVD remains the backbone of therapy in older adults and resource-limited settings due to its simplicity and lower acute toxicity ref [76]. Ongoing research continues to evaluate whether novel agents like brentuximab vedotin or checkpoint inhibitors can replace or augment these regimens, but ABVD and BEACOPP remain the benchmark against which new strategies are measured ref [58].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Landscapes: From Chemoradiation to Targeted and Immunotherapies
subsections.subsection_title: Role of radiotherapy: Evolution and current indications
subsections.content:
Radiotherapy (RT) has undergone a profound evolution in the management of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), shifting from a primary curative modality to a targeted, consolidative tool in the modern era. Historically, extended-field RT was standard after chemotherapy, but concerns over late toxicities—including secondary malignancies, cardiovascular disease, and pulmonary fibrosis—prompted a reduction in field size and dose. The introduction of combined modality therapy (CMT) with ABVD or BEACOPP allowed for lower RT doses (20–30 Gy) and involved-site RT (ISRT), minimizing exposure to uninvolved tissues while preserving efficacy. Contemporary guidelines now reserve RT primarily for patients with residual disease after chemotherapy, particularly those with bulky disease or positive interim PET-CT, where it significantly reduces relapse risk. The RATHL trial demonstrated that PET-adapted strategies can safely omit RT in patients achieving complete metabolic response, reducing long-term toxicity without compromising survival. Subsequent studies, including those from the German Hodgkin Study Group, confirmed that ISRT at 20–30 Gy is sufficient for consolidation in PET-positive cases, while PET-negative patients may avoid RT entirely. The role of RT has thus become highly selective, guided by response assessment and risk stratification.

Recent evidence supports the safety and efficacy of omitting RT in early-stage favorable cHL treated with ABVD, as shown in the HD15 and HD17 trials, where chemotherapy alone achieved comparable outcomes. In advanced-stage disease, RT is increasingly reserved for residual metabolic activity after frontline therapy, with ongoing trials evaluating whether novel agents like brentuximab vedotin or checkpoint inhibitors can further reduce RT dependence. The integration of PET-CT response criteria and the Deauville scoring system has been pivotal in refining RT indications, ensuring that only those with persistent disease receive radiation. This precision approach balances curative intent with the imperative to mitigate late effects, particularly in younger patients.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Landscapes: From Chemoradiation to Targeted and Immunotherapies
subsections.subsection_title: Brentuximab vedotin: Antibody-drug conjugate revolution
subsections.content:
Brentuximab vedotin (BV), an antibody-drug conjugate targeting CD30, marked a paradigm shift in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) therapy by delivering the microtubule-disrupting agent monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE) directly to Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells. Its approval was grounded in pivotal trials demonstrating high response rates in relapsed/refractory cHL, where conventional therapies had failed. The phase II study by Ansell et al. showed an overall response rate of 75% and a complete response rate of 34% in this heavily pretreated population, establishing BV as a transformative agent ref [19]. Subsequent phase III trials, including ECHELON-1, confirmed its efficacy in first-line settings when combined with AVD, significantly improving progression-free survival compared to ABVD, particularly in high-risk patients ref [19]. The favorable toxicity profile—predominantly peripheral neuropathy and neutropenia—distinguished BV from the cumulative myelosuppression of alkylating agents, enabling its integration into frontline regimens without compromising tolerability in elderly or frail patients ref [17].

BV’s success is underpinned by the near-universal overexpression of CD30 on malignant cells in cHL, a feature validated across multiple immunophenotypic studies ref [21]. Its mechanism exploits the tumor-specific antigen expression while sparing normal tissues, exemplifying the promise of targeted conjugates. Real-world evidence and long-term follow-up from phase I/II trials further support durable remissions and potential for cure in subsets of patients, reinforcing its role beyond salvage therapy ref [19]. The advent of BV not only expanded therapeutic options but also catalyzed the development of next-generation ADCs and combination strategies with immunotherapy, cementing its status as a cornerstone of modern cHL management.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Landscapes: From Chemoradiation to Targeted and Immunotherapies
subsections.subsection_title: Immune checkpoint inhibitors: PD-1 blockade in cHL
subsections.content:
The discovery of recurrent genetic alterations in chromosome 9p24.1, leading to amplified PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression in Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells, provided a compelling rationale for PD-1 blockade in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) [1]. This immune-evasive mechanism, coupled with a dense but dysfunctional tumor microenvironment, rendered cHL uniquely susceptible to immune checkpoint inhibition. Early phase I/II trials demonstrated remarkable response rates of 65–85% in patients with relapsed or refractory cHL, establishing nivolumab and pembrolizumab as transformative agents [2,3]. These responses were often durable, with some patients achieving long-term remission even after failure of autologous stem cell transplantation and brentuximab vedotin [4]. Subsequent studies confirmed efficacy across diverse patient populations, including those with primary refractory disease and post-transplant relapse [5]. The favorable toxicity profile—predominantly immune-related adverse events of low grade—further supported integration into clinical practice, particularly in settings where cytotoxic therapies are poorly tolerated [6].

Building on these findings, PD-1 inhibitors have been incorporated into frontline regimens, with trials evaluating combinations with chemotherapy (e.g., nivolumab plus AVD) showing improved progression-free survival compared to ABVD alone, while reducing the need for radiotherapy [7]. Emerging data suggest that tumor microenvironment composition, including CD8+ T-cell infiltration and interferon-gamma signaling, may predict response, offering potential for biomarker-driven selection [8]. Ongoing research is exploring PD-1 blockade in combination with novel agents, including epigenetic modulators and cellular therapies, to overcome primary and acquired resistance [9].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Landscapes: From Chemoradiation to Targeted and Immunotherapies
subsections.subsection_title: CAR T-cell therapy and novel cellular approaches
subsections.content:
CAR T-cell therapy has emerged as a promising salvage option for patients with relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) who fail PD-1 blockade and antibody-drug conjugates. Early-phase trials have demonstrated durable responses in a subset of heavily pretreated patients, leveraging the high expression of CD30 on Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells. A phase 1 study of anti-CD30 CAR T cells reported an overall response rate of 75%, with complete responses sustained beyond 12 months in some patients, highlighting the potential for long-term disease control ref [84]. However, challenges remain, including cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity, and limited persistence of infused cells in the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment ref [85].

Novel cellular approaches are being explored to overcome these limitations, including dual-targeting CAR constructs (e.g., CD30/CD19 or CD30/CD20) and armored CARs engineered to secrete cytokines such as IL-12 or express checkpoint inhibitors to enhance in vivo persistence ref [86]. Additionally, allogeneic off-the-shelf CAR T-cell products derived from healthy donors are under investigation to reduce manufacturing delays and costs ref [87]. Recent preclinical studies have also evaluated natural killer (NK) cell-based therapies targeting CD30 or CD16A, showing potent cytotoxicity against cHL cell lines without inducing severe toxicity ref [88].

Integration of single-cell transcriptomics has revealed T-cell exhaustion signatures in the cHL microenvironment, informing the design of next-generation cellular therapies that co-target inhibitory pathways such as TIM-3 or LAG-3 ref [29]. Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating CAR T cells in combination with PD-1 inhibitors to reinvigorate endogenous immunity ref [89]. While still investigational, these approaches represent a paradigm shift toward personalized, multi-pronged cellular immunotherapies for cHL.

subsections.section_title: Management of Relapsed and Refractory Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Salvage chemotherapy regimens: DHAP, ICE, GDP
subsections.content:
Salvage chemotherapy regimens such as DHAP (dexamethasone, cisplatin, cytarabine), ICE (ifosfamide, carboplatin, etoposide), and GDP (gemcitabine, dexamethasone, cisplatin) remain cornerstone options for patients with relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) prior to autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT). DHAP has demonstrated high response rates in prospective trials, particularly in patients with chemosensitive disease, and is often favored for its efficacy in achieving complete remission prior to transplant ref [90]. ICE, with its myelosuppressive profile, is commonly used in patients with prior anthracycline exposure or renal impairment, offering comparable efficacy to DHAP in retrospective analyses ref [91]. GDP has emerged as a less toxic alternative with favorable hematologic tolerability, showing non-inferior response rates in randomized comparisons and is increasingly adopted in elderly or frail populations ref [92]. A meta-analysis of salvage regimens confirmed that DHAP and ICE yield similar progression-free survival, while GDP offers reduced nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity without compromising efficacy ref [93]. The choice among these regimens is often guided by patient-specific factors including prior therapy, comorbidities, and institutional preference, rather than clear superiority of one regimen over another.

Recent studies have explored biomarkers to predict response to these regimens, with interim PET-CT after one or two cycles showing prognostic value for subsequent ASCT outcomes ref [56]. Although novel agents like brentuximab vedotin and checkpoint inhibitors are reshaping the salvage landscape, DHAP, ICE, and GDP continue to serve as the backbone for transplant-eligible patients due to their established efficacy and integration into standardized protocols ref [41]. Combination strategies, such as GDP with brentuximab, are under investigation to enhance depth of response, but conventional regimens remain the standard for conditioning prior to ASCT ref [94].

subsections.section_title: Management of Relapsed and Refractory Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Autologous vs. allogeneic stem cell transplantation
subsections.content:
Autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) remains the standard consolidative therapy for eligible patients with relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) who respond to salvage chemotherapy, offering durable remissions in approximately 50% of cases. ASCT is favored due to its lower non-relapse mortality compared to allogeneic transplantation, with long-term survival rates exceeding 40% in selected cohorts. However, relapse after ASCT remains common, particularly in patients with primary refractory disease or poor pre-transplant metabolic response, prompting consideration of allogeneic stem cell transplantation (allo-SCT) as a salvage option. Allo-SCT offers the potential for graft-versus-lymphoma effects and may induce durable remissions even in chemorefractory disease, with some studies reporting 5-year overall survival rates of 30–40%.

Despite its curative potential, allo-SCT is associated with higher treatment-related mortality (15–25%) due to graft-versus-host disease and infections, limiting its use to younger, fit patients with high-risk features or ASCT failure. Reduced-intensity conditioning regimens have expanded eligibility and improved safety, making allo-SCT a viable option for selected patients post-ASCT relapse. Comparative analyses suggest that allo-SCT may confer superior progression-free survival in high-risk subgroups, though overall survival benefit remains debated due to competing risks. Recent data support the use of allo-SCT after failure of novel agents such as brentuximab vedotin and checkpoint inhibitors, particularly in patients with persistent disease burden or adverse molecular features.

subsections.section_title: Management of Relapsed and Refractory Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Sequencing of novel agents: Brentuximab, checkpoint inhibitors, and beyond
subsections.content:
The sequencing of novel agents in relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) has evolved significantly, with brentuximab vedotin (BV) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) now forming the backbone of therapy. Brentuximab vedotin, an anti-CD30 antibody-drug conjugate, demonstrated durable responses in patients failing autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT), leading to its approval as a pre-transplant salvage and post-transplant maintenance option ref [89]. Subsequent studies established ICIs such as nivolumab and pembrolizumab as highly effective in BV-failed patients, with objective response rates exceeding 65% in both first- and later-line settings ref [68], ref [78]. The optimal sequencing remains debated, but emerging evidence supports ICI use prior to ASCT in BV-naïve patients to improve transplant eligibility and depth of response ref [43]. Combination strategies, including BV plus nivolumab, have shown high response rates in early-phase trials, suggesting potential for chemo-free regimens ref [33]. Beyond these agents, novel approaches targeting alternative immune checkpoints (e.g., LAG-3, TIGIT), PI3Kδ inhibitors, and epigenetic modulators are under active investigation ref [93], ref [79].

Resistance to BV and ICIs is increasingly recognized as multifactorial, involving downregulation of CD30 expression, loss of antigen presentation, and adaptive upregulation of alternative immune checkpoints ref [80], ref [65]. Recent genomic analyses of relapsed samples reveal clonal evolution in PD-L1/L2 loci and mutations in JAK-STAT and NF-κB pathways that may drive escape ref [50], ref [37]. These insights are informing next-generation strategies, including bispecific antibodies, CAR T cells targeting CD30 or CD19, and IL-12-secreting armored CAR T cells designed to overcome the immunosuppressive microenvironment ref [24], ref [25], ref [33]. The integration of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for real-time monitoring is enabling dynamic treatment adjustments, potentially guiding sequential therapy based on molecular response ref [31], ref [67].

subsections.section_title: Management of Relapsed and Refractory Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Emerging resistance mechanisms and therapeutic escape
subsections.content:
Emerging resistance to novel agents in relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is driven by complex mechanisms of immune evasion and tumor cell adaptation. Persistent PD-1 blockade can select for clones with JAK2 mutations or amplifications of 9p24.1, leading to constitutive JAK-STAT signaling and upregulation of PD-L1/L2 independent of interferon signaling, thereby sustaining immune escape ref [66]. Genomic instability in Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells facilitates clonal evolution, with ctDNA profiling revealing subclonal emergence of mutations in B2M, CIITA, and HLA genes that impair antigen presentation ref [16]. Epigenetic silencing of MHC class II molecules via CIITA promoter methylation further diminishes T-cell recognition ref [50]. The tumor microenvironment contributes through upregulation of alternative immune checkpoints such as TIM-3, LAG-3, and TIGIT, which compensate for PD-1 inhibition ref [27]. Additionally, metabolic reprogramming of tumor cells, including increased glycolysis and tryptophan catabolism via IDO1, creates an immunosuppressive niche ref [70]. Resistance to CD30-targeted therapies like brentuximab vedotin may arise from reduced CD30 expression, lysosomal sequestration of the drug, or activation of PI3K/AKT survival pathways ref [24]. Single-cell transcriptomics has identified exhausted T-cell subsets with co-expression of multiple inhibitory receptors, suggesting a need for combinatorial checkpoint blockade ref [91].

Recent proteogenomic analyses have uncovered novel resistance drivers, including dysregulation of NF-κB and NOTCH signaling networks that promote survival despite targeted inhibition ref [82]. Furthermore, regulatory B cells and myeloid-derived suppressor cells within the microenvironment actively suppress cytotoxic T-cell function, enabling therapeutic escape ref [85]. These findings underscore the necessity of multi-modal therapeutic strategies that simultaneously target tumor-intrinsic alterations and microenvironmental immunosuppression.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Personalized Medicine, Novel Targets, and Global Health Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Targeting novel pathways: LMP1, CD40, and epigenetic modulators
subsections.content:
The latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1) of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is expressed in a subset of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) cases and drives constitutive NF-κB and JAK/STAT signaling, promoting survival of Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells. Targeting LMP1 directly remains challenging, but downstream effectors such as TRAF proteins and IKK complexes are under investigation as indirect therapeutic nodes. CD40, a TNF receptor superfamily member overexpressed on HRS cells, engages with CD40L on tumor-associated T cells to sustain pro-survival signals and cytokine production; preclinical studies demonstrate that CD40 blockade or agonistic antibodies can disrupt this axis and restore immune recognition [CD40 signaling promotes survival of Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells in the microenvironment]. Epigenetic dysregulation is a hallmark of cHL, with recurrent mutations in CREBBP and EP300 leading to impaired histone acetylation and silencing of immune-related genes such as CIITA and B2M [CREBBP and EP300 mutations in classical Hodgkin lymphoma disrupt acetylation and immune recognition]. Inhibitors of histone deacetylases (HDACs) and EZH2 have shown preclinical efficacy in restoring MHC class II expression and enhancing T-cell recognition [Epigenetic silencing of CIITA in Hodgkin lymphoma contributes to MHC class II downregulation]. Combined targeting of these pathways—LMP1-driven signaling, CD40 costimulation, and epigenetic modifiers—may overcome microenvironment-mediated immune evasion and synergize with checkpoint blockade.

Recent work has identified that HDAC inhibitors reverse the epigenetic silencing of tumor suppressor genes and enhance antigen presentation in HRS cells, while EZH2 inhibition reduces proliferation and sensitizes cells to apoptosis [Chromatin remodeling defects in Hodgkin lymphoma reveal therapeutic vulnerabilities]. Dual targeting of CD40 and PD-1 has demonstrated enhanced T-cell activation in murine models, suggesting combinatorial potential. Moreover, CRISPR-based screens have uncovered novel epigenetic dependencies in EBV+ cHL, highlighting vulnerabilities in chromatin remodeling complexes that may be exploited therapeutically [Integrated genomic and epigenomic profiling of classical Hodgkin lymphoma identifies novel driver alterations]. These emerging strategies represent a shift toward precision targeting of oncogenic drivers beyond conventional cytotoxic regimens.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Personalized Medicine, Novel Targets, and Global Health Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Combination immunotherapies and bispecific antibodies
subsections.content:
Combination immunotherapies and bispecific antibodies represent a promising frontier in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) treatment, aiming to overcome resistance to single-agent PD-1 blockade by simultaneously targeting multiple immune evasion mechanisms. Bispecific T-cell engagers (BiTEs) targeting CD30 and CD3 have demonstrated potent in vitro and in vivo activity against Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells, with early-phase trials showing clinical responses in relapsed/refractory patients. Combinations of PD-1 inhibitors with novel agents such as LAG-3 or TIM-3 blockade are being explored to reverse T-cell exhaustion within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Additionally, dual-targeting bispecific antibodies engaging both CD30 and CD16a on natural killer cells have shown enhanced antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity in preclinical models. The integration of these approaches with epigenetic modulators may further restore antigen presentation and enhance immune recognition, as suggested by recent findings on CIITA silencing and MHC class II downregulation.

Clinical trials are now evaluating sequential and concurrent regimens, including PD-1 blockade combined with CD30-directed CAR T cells or bispecific antibodies, to amplify cytotoxic T-cell infiltration and sustain antitumor immunity. Early data from phase I/II studies indicate that such combinations are feasible and may yield deeper and more durable responses than monotherapies, particularly in patients with high tumor burden or prior exposure to brentuximab vedotin. Ongoing research is focused on identifying biomarkers predictive of response and mitigating cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity associated with T-cell redirection strategies.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Personalized Medicine, Novel Targets, and Global Health Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Artificial intelligence in diagnosis and outcome prediction
subsections.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the diagnosis and outcome prediction in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) by enabling high-accuracy analysis of complex multimodal data. Deep learning models applied to histopathology slides have demonstrated performance comparable to expert pathologists in identifying Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells, leveraging convolutional neural networks trained on large-scale digitized tissue datasets ref [62]. AI-driven image analysis of PET-CT scans is increasingly used to automate Deauville score assignment, reducing inter-observer variability and improving consistency in response assessment ref [33]. Furthermore, machine learning algorithms integrating clinical, genomic, and imaging features have been developed to predict treatment response and relapse risk with greater precision than traditional staging systems ref [75].

Recent studies have shown that AI models incorporating circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) dynamics and transcriptomic profiles can identify molecular signatures of early relapse prior to radiographic progression, enabling preemptive intervention ref [96]. One study utilized random forest classifiers to combine serial ctDNA levels with baseline gene expression data, achieving an AUC of 0.92 for relapse prediction in early-stage cHL ref [100]. Additionally, natural language processing models have been trained to extract prognostic information from unstructured electronic health records, enhancing risk stratification in resource-limited settings ref [97]. These advances underscore AI’s potential to personalize therapy and optimize surveillance strategies, though validation in diverse, multiethnic cohorts remains critical to ensure generalizability.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Personalized Medicine, Novel Targets, and Global Health Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Global disparities in cHL care
subsections.content:
Global disparities in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) care remain profound, with survival rates varying dramatically between high-income and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). In high-income regions, 5-year survival exceeds 90%, whereas in many LMICs, it falls below 50% due to delayed diagnosis, limited access to diagnostic pathology, and inadequate treatment infrastructure. In sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia, advanced-stage disease is common at presentation, partly due to lack of awareness and fragmented healthcare systems ref [73]. Diagnostic delays are exacerbated by the scarcity of immunohistochemical tools needed to confirm cHL, particularly in resource-limited settings where PAX5 and CD30 staining are often unavailable ref [92].

Treatment access is further hindered by the high cost and logistical complexity of first-line regimens like ABVD and BEACOPP, as well as newer agents such as brentuximab vedotin and immune checkpoint inhibitors. In many LMICs, chemotherapy shortages, unreliable drug supply chains, and absence of supportive care (e.g., granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) lead to increased toxicity and treatment abandonment ref [17]. Additionally, radiotherapy, a critical component of modern cHL management, is inaccessible in over 60% of LMICs due to a lack of linear accelerators and trained personnel ref [73].

Efforts to address these inequities include WHO initiatives to strengthen cancer control in LMICs and regional collaborations to standardize diagnostic protocols. However, sustainable solutions require investment in local pathology capacity, affordable generic drug procurement, and integration of cHL into national non-communicable disease programs ref [73]. Without systemic intervention, the global survival gap in cHL will persist despite therapeutic advances in high-resource settings.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Personalized Medicine, Novel Targets, and Global Health Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Prevention and early detection strategies
subsections.content:
Prevention and early detection of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) remain underexplored frontiers, despite known associations with infectious and environmental risk factors. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is a well-established etiological agent in a subset of cHL cases, particularly in mixed cellularity subtypes and in low-resource settings, suggesting that EBV vaccination or antiviral strategies could reduce incidence in high-risk populations ref [14]. Familial clustering and genetic predisposition, including polymorphisms in HLA and immune-related genes, further support the potential for risk stratification ref [71]. Epidemiological studies have linked modifiable factors such as obesity and smoking to increased cHL risk, offering opportunities for public health interventions ref [86]. Early detection remains challenging due to the nonspecific presentation of symptoms, but emerging liquid biopsy approaches using circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) show promise in identifying molecular relapse before clinical manifestation ref [41]. Serum proteomic signatures have also been proposed as non-invasive biomarkers for early disease detection, though validation in prospective cohorts is still needed ref [42]. Integrating population-based screening with genomic and serological risk profiling may enable targeted surveillance in high-risk individuals, particularly in regions with rising cHL incidence.

Advances in single-cell transcriptomics and machine learning have begun to uncover pre-malignant immune microenvironment alterations preceding overt cHL, potentially enabling interception at the premalignant stage ref [44]. Longitudinal studies tracking immune dysregulation in EBV-seropositive individuals with genetic risk factors may identify predictive signatures for early intervention. However, global disparities in access to diagnostic tools and genetic screening limit the scalability of such strategies, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where cHL incidence is rising and healthcare infrastructure is limited.
